newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu-Kabila to meet on Friday-U.S. envoy.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu-Kabila to meet on Friday-U.S. envoy.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson said on Wednesday Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila agreed to hold their first face-to-face meeting on Friday on a South African ship in the Atlantic.
"The meeting will take place on Friday on a South African ship. The ship will be sailing from Libreville into international waters," he said after one hour and 40 minutes of talks with Mobutu.
"Hopefully it will lead to peace in Zaire," the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations told reporters in Kinshasa.
He added that several African leaders and joint U.N. and Organisation of African Unity envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would be present on the South African navy ship for the talks on Friday.
It would be the first direct meeting between the ailing Zairean president and Kabila, whose rebels have seized more than half of Zaire since October and are advancing on Kinshasa.

Richardson was flanked by Zairean Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda. Mobutu, looking gaunt and thin, stood behind him briefly in the doorway of the presidential villa in the heavily guarded Tshatshi military camp on the banks of the Zaire river.
Asked what caused Mobutu's change of heart, Kamanda said: "It was a perception of the higher interest of the nation."
Mobutu had said that he preferred a meeting in Gabon, which was rejected by Kabila.

"I want to commend the statesmanlike action of President Mobutu and Mr Kabila in accepting these talks," said Richardson, adding Mobutu gave him a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton in response to one he had delivered on Tuesday.
"It is our hope there will be a ceasefire while these talks take place," Richardson said. But he added this was a step-by -step process. Kabila has ruled out a ceasefire before talks.
Richardson said part of the agreement was that he should attend the beginning of the talks and added in the next two days he might go on to South Africa, Gabon and possibly Angola.
Asked what the agenda for the talks was, Richardson said that would be discussed at the face-to-face encounter. Kabila has said he wanted only a brief meeting to discuss Mobutu's stepping down.
Earlier on Wednesday, Kabila appealed to the international community to force Mobutu to attend talks at sea to avoid a battle for Kinshasa, the teeming capital of five million people.

"We remain committed to the talks despite our military advantage but the international community must now put pressure on Mobutu and force him to come to talks at sea," Kabila told Reuters in Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi.

A diplomat travelling with Richardson said on Tuesday that Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August and met Richardson on Tuesdday, had turned down a South African offer to host talks at sea off Zaire on a South African ship.
Kabila told Reuters on Wednesday that he would not go to Gabon, the venue preferred by Mobutu, for security reasons and would only meet Mobutu on the ship offered by President Nelson Mandela.
